title: Control Systems
tagline: Modelling, transient response, stability, root locus, frequency response, compensation and state space
summary: Feedback lets a system follow commands and reject disturbances despite uncertainty. This course models dynamic systems, analyses their transient response and stability, designs controllers with the root-locus and frequency-response methods, introduces state-space models and state feedback, and implements controllers digitally.
overview: A control system measures what a process is doing, compares it with what it should be doing, and acts on the difference. The thermostat in a soldering station, the current loop inside a motor drive, the voltage loop of a laptop's power supply, the pitch servo of a wind turbine and the phase-locked loop of a radio are all **feedback systems**, and nearly every one of them is built from electrical sensors, electrical actuators and an analog or digital controller. Feedback lets a cheap, uncertain plant behave like an accurate one, suppresses disturbances such as load changes and supply ripple, and can even stabilise a process that is unstable on its own. Badly designed, the same feedback makes a system ring, drift or oscillate.

The course follows the classical route and then the modern one. We first build models — transfer functions and block diagrams of circuits, DC motors and power converters, linearised where the physics is nonlinear — and learn how pole positions set the transient response and the steady-state error. Stability is decided algebraically with the Routh–Hurwitz criterion, then graphically: the **root locus** shows how the closed-loop poles move as a gain is raised, and the **Bode and Nyquist** plots of the loop gain give gain and phase margins that can be measured on real hardware. With these tools we design PID controllers and lead–lag compensators, realised with op-amps or in software. The last three chapters work in the time domain with **state-space** models, place every closed-loop pole by state feedback, estimate unmeasured states with observers, and finally implement controllers on a microcontroller, where sampling, delay and quantisation enter the loop.

Control is hard for two reasons. The mathematics links three views of one system — differential equations in time, poles and zeros in the $s$-plane, and frequency responses — and design means moving fluently between them. And every real loop involves trade-offs that no formula resolves for you: speed against overshoot, disturbance rejection against noise sensitivity, performance against robustness to a plant you do not know exactly. Work each example numerically, sketch before you compute, and check every design by simulating its step response. The Mechanical Engineering Atlas has a companion course on control with a mechanical emphasis; this one takes the electrical engineer's view of the same theory.
outcomes: Derive transfer-function and block-diagram models of electrical, electromechanical and power-electronic systems, and linearise nonlinear models about an operating point.
Predict the step response of first- and second-order systems from their poles and zeros, and compute rise time, overshoot, settling time and steady-state error.
Determine the stability of a feedback system and the range of gains for which it is stable using pole locations and the Routh–Hurwitz criterion.
Sketch root loci with the construction rules and use them to choose gains and place compensator poles and zeros.
Construct Bode and Nyquist plots of a loop gain, apply the Nyquist criterion, and compute gain, phase and delay margins.
Design and tune PID controllers, including cascade current and speed loops for motor drives, and protect them against integrator windup and derivative kick.
Design lead, lag and lead–lag compensators to meet transient, steady-state and margin specifications, and realise them with op-amp circuits.
Formulate state-space models, solve them with the matrix exponential, convert between state-space and transfer-function forms, and test controllability and observability.
Design state-feedback controllers and observers by pole placement, explain the separation principle, and solve a simple linear-quadratic regulator problem.
Discretise continuous controllers and plants, analyse sampled-data loops in the $z$-plane, and implement a controller in fixed-rate software accounting for delay and quantisation.

chapters.title: Modelling dynamic systems
chapters.summary: Transfer functions and block diagrams of electrical, mechanical and electromechanical systems, and linearisation.

chapters.title: Time response
chapters.summary: First- and second-order responses, transient specifications, the effect of zeros and extra poles, and steady-state error.

chapters.title: Stability
chapters.summary: Bounded-input bounded-output stability, the Routh–Hurwitz criterion and the stability of feedback systems.

chapters.title: Root locus
chapters.summary: Sketching the root locus and using it to choose gains and design compensators.

chapters.title: Frequency-response methods
chapters.summary: Bode plots of open-loop systems, the Nyquist criterion, and gain and phase margins.

chapters.title: PID control
chapters.summary: Proportional, integral and derivative action, tuning rules, integrator windup and practical PID implementation.

chapters.title: Lead and lag compensation
chapters.summary: Design of lead, lag and lead–lag compensators with the root locus and Bode plots.

chapters.title: State-space models
chapters.summary: State equations, solutions with the matrix exponential, and controllability and observability.

chapters.title: State feedback and observers
chapters.summary: Pole placement, state observers, the separation principle and an introduction to optimal control.

chapters.title: Digital control
chapters.summary: Sampled-data systems, discretisation of controllers, z-domain design and implementation effects.

history.title: Maxwell's 'On governors'
history.detail: James Clerk Maxwell linearised the equations of centrifugal speed governors and showed that their stability depends on the signs of the real parts of the roots of a characteristic equation.

history.title: Routh's stability criterion
history.detail: Edward Routh's Adams Prize essay gave a tabular test for whether all roots of a polynomial have negative real parts; Adolf Hurwitz found an equivalent determinant condition independently in 1895.

history.title: Three-term control of ship steering
history.detail: Nicolas Minorsky analysed automatic steering of ships and proposed a controller with proportional, integral and derivative terms, the theoretical origin of PID control.

history.title: The Nyquist criterion
history.detail: Harry Nyquist's paper 'Regeneration theory' showed how to decide closed-loop stability from the open-loop frequency response, building on Harold Black's negative-feedback amplifier of 1927.

history.title: Bode's gain–phase relations
history.detail: Hendrik Bode related the attenuation and phase of minimum-phase networks and introduced gain and phase margins; his 1945 book made frequency-response design standard practice.

history.title: Ziegler–Nichols tuning rules
history.detail: John Ziegler and Nathaniel Nichols of Taylor Instrument Companies published empirical rules for setting the gains of PID process controllers from a step test or the ultimate gain.

history.title: The root-locus method
history.detail: Walter Evans published 'Graphical analysis of control systems', introducing the root locus as a way of seeing how closed-loop poles move with gain; his 1950 paper applied it to synthesis.

history.title: z-transform analysis of sampled-data systems
history.detail: John Ragazzini and Lotfi Zadeh at Columbia University introduced the z-transform as the standard tool for analysing control systems with sampled signals.

history.title: State-space control theory
history.detail: Rudolf Kálmán introduced controllability and observability, the linear-quadratic regulator and, with the Kalman filter, optimal state estimation, founding modern state-space control.

history.title: Observers
history.detail: David Luenberger showed how to reconstruct the state of a linear system from its inputs and outputs with a dynamic observer, completing the toolkit for output-feedback design by pole placement.

references.title: Control Systems Engineering
references.note: The most widely used first course text (8th edition): very clear on modelling, time response, root locus and frequency response, with many electrical and electromechanical case studies.

references.title: Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems
references.authors: Gene F. Franklin, J. David Powell, Abbas Emami-Naeini
references.note: Rigorous and design-oriented (8th edition); excellent on root locus, frequency-response design, state-space methods and digital implementation.

references.title: Modern Control Engineering
references.note: A classic (5th edition) with many fully worked problems on transient response, PID tuning, lead–lag design and state space.

references.title: Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers
references.authors: Karl J. Åström, Richard M. Murray
references.note: A modern treatment (2nd edition, freely available online) that emphasises robustness, the sensitivity functions and the limits of performance.

references.title: Digital Control of Dynamic Systems
references.authors: Gene F. Franklin, J. David Powell, Michael L. Workman
references.note: The standard reference on sampled-data control (3rd edition): discretisation, z-plane design, quantisation and sample-rate selection.

references.title: Advanced PID Control
references.note: Everything practical about PID controllers: tuning rules, windup, filtering, setpoint weighting and implementation.

references.title: Fundamentals of Power Electronics
references.note: Chapters on averaged converter models and feedback loop design (3rd edition) show the control of switching power supplies, including right-half-plane zeros and Type II/III compensators.
